Cockatrice
KOK-uh-tris
noun
From Old French cocatris, through Latin calcatrix (a tracker or treader), used to render a deadly serpent. It translates Hebrew tsepha’ / tsiph’oni, a poisonous viper or adder, more venomous than the common asp.

Biblical Definition

The cockatrice is the KJV’s word for a most venomous serpent, an adder or viper whose bite was reckoned deadly beyond healing—in later legend a fabled creature that killed with a look, but in Scripture simply the fiercest of the poisonous snakes. It appears in prophecy both as a terror and, marvelously, as a token of restored peace. In Isaiah’s vision of the Messiah’s reign, the enmity of the serpent is undone: the weaned child shall put his hand on the cockatrice’ den (Isa 11:8), the most helpless creature made safe over the deadliest, for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD. Elsewhere the cockatrice is a figure of judgment breeding judgment: out of the serpent’s root shall come forth a cockatrice, and his fruit shall be a fiery flying serpent (Isa 14:29), Philistia warned that a worse foe follows the one now broken. Isaiah lays it upon the works of the wicked, who hatch cockatrice’ eggs, and weave the spider’s web: he that eateth of their eggs dieth (Isa 59:5)—their schemes are venom, deadly to whoever partakes of them. And Jeremiah makes it the very instrument of the LORD’s wrath: I will send serpents, cockatrices, among you, which will not be charmed, and they shall bite you, saith the LORD (Jer 8:17). The cockatrice thus preaches two truths that meet only in Christ. Sin is a serpent’s brood, venomous, self-propagating, uncharmed by any human wisdom; but the Seed of the woman shall bruise the serpent’s head, and in His kingdom the weaned child plays unharmed upon the viper’s den, the old enmity swallowed up in peace.

Webster 1828 Definition

A most venomous serpent, an adder or viper; in legend a fabled creature deadly to sight.

expand to see more

COCKATRICE, n. [Old Fr. cocatris; L. calcatrix, a treader.] A serpent of the most venomous kind; an adder or viper whose bite is deadly.

In fable, a monstrous creature hatched from a cock’s egg, said to kill by its very look or breath.

In Scripture, it renders the Hebrew for a poisonous viper, more deadly than the common asp (Isa. lix. 5; Jer. viii. 17).

A figure of judgment and of the venomous devices of the wicked, that will not be charmed nor turned aside.

In the prophecy of the Messiah’s reign, the tamed terror upon whose den the weaned child lays his hand unharmed (Isa. xi. 8).

Key Scripture

Isa 11:8 — "And the sucking child shall play on the hole of the asp, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the cockatrice' den."

Isa 14:29 — "Rejoice not thou, whole Palestina, because the rod of him that smote thee is broken: for out of the serpent's root shall come forth a cockatrice, and his fruit shall be a fiery flying serpent."

Isa 59:5 — "They hatch cockatrice' eggs, and weave the spider's web: he that eateth of their eggs dieth, and that which is crushed breaketh out into a viper."

Jer 8:17 — "For, behold, I will send serpents, cockatrices, among you, which will not be charmed, and they shall bite you, saith the LORD."

Modern Corruption

Not a contested doctrine but a name for a deadly serpent; it recovers the venom of sin and the serpent-crushing peace of the Messiah’s reign.

expand to see more

The age is content to smile at the cockatrice as a quaint monster of old bestiaries and to miss the deadly earnest of the thing it names. Scripture uses it soberly: the schemes of the wicked are cockatrice’ eggs, and whoever feeds on them dies; the LORD’s judgment is a brood of serpents that will not be charmed by any spell of human cunning. The modern mind, having ceased to believe in the venom of sin, is forever surprised when the eggs it warmed hatch into vipers. To hatch cockatrice’ eggs and expect no poison is the folly Isaiah rebukes.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that sin is a serpent’s brood—venomous, self-propagating, uncharmed by wisdom or will—and that its enmity is undone in one place only. In the reign of the Messiah the weaned child lays his hand upon the cockatrice’ den and is not hurt, for the Seed of the woman has bruised the serpent’s head. The same word that names the deadliest terror names, in Christ’s kingdom, the terror at last made harmless.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

A word for a deadly viper rooted in the Old French and Latin for a treading serpent.

expand to see more

Old French cocatris, from Latin calcatrix—a tracker or treader, applied to a deadly serpent.

Hebrew tsepha’ / tsiph’oni—a poisonous viper or adder, more venomous than the common asp.

In later legend, a fabled monster hatched from a cock’s egg, said to slay by a look.

A figure of the wicked’s devices—cockatrice’ eggs that bring death to whoever eats of them.

Tamed at last in the Messiah’s reign, its den made a safe playground for the weaned child.

Usage

"They hatch cockatrice’ eggs who warm their evil schemes and are then astonished at the venom."

"The LORD’s judgment came as cockatrices that would not be charmed by any human cunning."

"In the kingdom of the Prince of Peace the weaned child plays unharmed upon the cockatrice’ den."
